synopsis: On a BCO 41 reference, the SJC tried a minister on seven charges arising from allegations of sexual misconduct, bullying, dishonesty, a civil defamation suit, contumacy, doctrinal error, and lack of fitness. It found him not guilty on every charge because the prosecution failed to meet its burden, removed all censures and administrative suspensions, and restored him to good standing. For the lawsuit charge, it rejected a categorical ban on civil suits between Christians and required proof that this suit was sinful.

synopsis: An indicted teaching elder challenged Chesapeake Presbytery’s approval of a PJC judgment and indefinite suspension after the PJC blended a BCO 32 case of process with a BCO 38-1 case without process. The SJC sustained the complaint, annulled Presbytery’s approval, and returned the matter to the PJC. Because he admitted only some indicted charges, his negotiated confession could not satisfy BCO 38-1 and the conversion prejudiced his rights. The PJC may dismiss or proceed under BCO 32; the ruling does not decide whether conversion is ever permissible.

synopsis: Did Heritage Presbytery err by cautioning a session and requesting that it postpone a candidate's election or ordination while a complaint about his qualifications was pending? The SJC said no and denied the complaint. The motion was advice, not an act for or requirement imposed on the session; the session could disregard it, and BCO 43-2 does not bar presbyters from discussing matters related to a complaint not yet before them. The SJC left undecided whether such discussions would disqualify presbyters, since the Ullrey complaint never reached presbytery.

topics: fundamentals of the system of doctrine
synopsis: An SJC complaint alleged that Ohio Valley Presbytery failed to comply with the SJC's prior remand in Case 2014-01, which required it to 'hear further' from TE Charles Hickey about his changed view on Larger Catechism 177. The SJC denied the complaint. It held that the prior decision neither sustained nor denied the original complaint and prescribed no particular examination procedure; Hickey's nine pages of additional affirmations, exegesis, and answers constituted hearing further, and he addressed the five identified areas at least in part. A concurrence believed the SJC could also have adjudicated the confessional-difference merits; a dissent would have found noncompliance and reached the merits.

title: Barnes v. Heartland Presbytery
topics: fundamentals of the system of doctrine
synopsis: Heartland Presbytery granted a transferring OPC teaching elder an exception to WCF 19, judging his stated differences 'more than semantic but not out of accord with any fundamental.' The SJC sustained a complaint not against the merits of that judgment but against the sufficiency of the record supporting it. It held Presbytery clearly erred by failing to develop a sufficient record: the presbyters as a whole did not receive OPCUS's adverse actions, its teaching restriction, or the elder's longer paper. Remanded for those materials and release documentation to be included in the minutes. A concurrence addressed deference; four dissenters found no clear error.

title: Aven and Dively v. Ohio Valley Presbytery
topics: fundamentals of the system of doctrine
synopsis: Two ministers complained that Ohio Valley Presbytery erred by judging TE Charles Hickey's difference with Larger Catechism 177—over restricting the Lord's Supper to those able to examine themselves—as more than semantic but neither hostile to the system nor vital to religion. The SJC neither sustained nor denied the complaint. Because the Record did not sufficiently address Hickey's particular expression and rationale, the Commission remanded to Presbytery for further hearing and a fuller record. It reserved the merits, including whether this formulation of paedocommunion is allowable.

synopsis: Teaching and ruling elders challenged Presbytery’s approval of TE Gregory Lawrence’s acquittal on five doctrinal charges. The SJC sustained the complaint on procedural grounds: the trial commission relied on his post-indictment exculpatory writings while he declined to testify, depriving the prosecution of cross-examination. The SJC ordered a new trial on the same indictment under specified evidentiary procedures. Because this was a complaint rather than an appeal, it did not reverse the acquittals into findings of guilt or decide the doctrinal merits.

synopsis: The SJC denied RE Gerald Hedman's complaint against Pacific Northwest Presbytery, which had adopted five not-guilty judgments on charges that TE Peter Leithart's baptism, covenant, imputation, justification, and union-with-Christ views contradicted the Westminster Standards. Bound to the record and clear-error review, the SJC found no procedural violation and insufficient evidence that Presbytery clearly erred. It left the verdicts undisturbed, declined to endorse Leithart's views generally, and urged continued clarification of his non-standard terminology. A separate dissent would have found error and ordered a new trial or reference.

synopsis: Brown challenged Presbytery’s abstract approval of six views concerning diaconal practice. The SJC sustained the consolidated complaints and annulled Presbytery’s action because a church court cannot issue a binding decree apart from properly exercising jurisdiction over specific persons. Constitutional conformity must instead be determined through authorized examination or judicial processes. The judgment deliberately left unresolved whether any of the six views themselves were faithful to the Constitution; the detailed view-by-view analysis appeared only in a concurring opinion.

title: Phelps v. Pacific Presbytery
synopsis: Phelps complained that Pacific Presbytery erred by finding no constitutional irregularities in the New Life Burbank Session's ordination of Lee Irons as a ruling elder, despite PP's earlier refusal to receive Irons as a teaching-elder candidate. The SJC denied the complaint. Under BCO 39-3.3, the Court owed great deference to the lower court's discretionary fitness judgment; the single office of elder does not require identical eligibility processes, and the NLB Session had jurisdiction after Irons renounced OPC jurisdiction. PP's action stood; the SJC declined to decide the NAPARC issue.

The SJC sustained a complaint, holding PNW erred because, without formal judicial process, it lacked authority to declare either that the views were out of accord or that they were not. The record still suggested a strong presumption of guilt. The SJC refused complainants' affirmative declaration and remanded with directions for pastoral counsel under BCO 31-7 and possible BCO 31-2 compliance.

synopsis: The complaint challenged Presbytery’s commissions and its response to a canceled congregational meeting. The SJC upheld the Inman Commission because a Session may reference limited duties without congregational consent. It sustained the challenges to Presbytery’s consideration of the August 7 meeting and appointment of the Sealy Commission because the Session majority had validly canceled the meeting. Linton’s and Pellom’s calls therefore remained undissolved and Neville was uncalled, absent later congregational action. The SJC also upheld Presbytery’s criticism of the cancellation as unwise and its refusal to issue a BCO 40-5 citation.

It also held that BCO 31-2 prescribes no interview requirement or fixed timeline and found no clear constitutional error warranting departure from ordinary deference to Presbytery.

synopsis: Smith challenged Presbytery’s reversal of a finding that an elder’s race-and-IQ views did not create a strong presumption of guilt and its immediate judgment against those views. The SJC upheld the reversal as a discretionary determination, without addressing its merits, but annulled the declaration against the views because a strong-presumption finding required judicial process. On remand, Presbytery was to commence process against the elder or rescind that finding and drop the matter. The ruling did not restrict Presbytery’s ability to adopt general position statements outside an investigation.

synopsis: The SJC denied James Urish and others' complaint against Rocky Mountain Presbytery for sustaining Dan Breed's ordination exam. Breed had said women could teach Scripture to mixed adults in settings like Sunday school under session oversight, but not preach, hold elder office, or teach outside session authority. Because the Westminster Standards and BCO did not expressly resolve that view, the SJC found no clear error under BCO 39 and affirmed Presbytery's denial. A concurrence criticized Breed's exegesis of 1 Tim. 2:12 but stressed the SJC was not endorsing it.

synopsis: On complaint from TE David Kniseley and others, the SJC reviewed Rocky Mountain Presbytery's refusal to forbid a mission church from giving an unordained female staff member the title 'Minister of Church Life.' The SJC denied the complaint. It held the BCO uses 'minister' synonymously with pastor and teaching elder, but is silent on general use for non-ordained staff; a lower court may exercise discretion subject to BCO 40-2(3)'s WESP review. The decision addressed only the constitutional issue, not the title's wisdom or propriety; four commissioners dissented.

synopsis: A minister appealed convictions and indefinite suspension arising from conflict over Presbytery's direction that he resign. The SJC upheld all three convictions, finding two procedural errors nonprejudicial and rejecting the other preserved challenges. But Presbytery could not treat its authority to dissolve a pastoral relationship as authority to compel resignation on pain of discipline. The SJC therefore vacated the censure and dissolution of the call and remanded for reconsideration of censure; Grady's separate administrative suspension remained effective.

synopsis: Two consolidated complaints challenged Philadelphia Presbytery’s licensing and ordination of a candidate who believed Scripture could permit women to hold the deacon’s office but promised to follow the BCO and not ordain women. The SJC denied both complaints and affirmed Presbytery. It distinguished subscription to doctrinal standards from approval of BCO practices, applied a three-part inquiry, and deferred to Presbytery on the candidate’s credible vow. Because complainants identified no violated doctrinal standard, no error was shown. The ruling reaffirmed that the BCO bars ordaining women as deacons.

synopsis: Louisiana Presbytery’s refusal to institute process after examining Steve Wilkins’s Federal Vision teachings was challenged for applying the wrong constitutional standard and overlooking a strong presumption that some views were out of conformity with the Westminster Standards. The SJC sustained the complaint and annulled Presbytery’s denial. A “difference” need not expressly contradict the Standards; Presbytery must independently investigate and classify it rather than accept the member’s assurance or shift the burden to objectors. synopsis: Bowen challenged Presbytery’s attempt, two years after installation, to rescind its earlier ruling and annul local officers’ elections and ordinations without trial. The SJC sustained the complaint: ordination is perpetual, deposition requires judicial process, and rescission was out of order after implementation; Presbytery likewise could not suspend a local elder without due process. But it affirmed that infant baptism and limited atonement are fundamentals admitting no officer exception. The officers remained in office but doctrinally out of accord; voluntary demission or proper process was advised.

The continued-noncompliance specification was sustained, but allegations of constitutional violation and contumacy were not sustained. Remedial recommendations were adopted, although the supplied excerpt provides neither their terms nor the deciding body’s reasons. The mixed ruling therefore distinguishes noncompliance from the complainants’ more serious characterizations of Presbytery’s conduct.

synopsis: The General Assembly sustained a complaint against Ascension Presbytery for sustaining a candidate's ordination trials despite exceptions to PCA constitutional standards. The Commission upheld specifications that his Lord's Supper and baptism views denied required visible-church membership and that his women-deacons view conflicted with the BCO; it rejected specifications on Sabbath recreation and immersion. The Assembly annulled the Presbytery's sustaining action, but not the ordination itself, so the candidate remained on the roll. It directed correction of the trial and pastoral instruction, with possible discipline if his views persisted.

title: Pastoral Oversight and Discipline in Marital Discord When Parties Are Under Different Jurisdictions
summary: CCB advised that no constitutional obstacle prevents courts from different presbyteries cooperating in marital reconciliation, though the BCO makes no provision for joint commissions of separate courts.

title: Procedure for Suspending Rules
summary: The CCB advised that delegates are bound to follow the Constitution as fully as possible and declined to affirm that rules must be suspended to obey Christ, directing any changes through proper amendment procedures.

title: Call of assistant pastor from another denomination without presbyterial examination
summary: A session may not call an ordained assistant pastor from another denomination without presbytery approval and examination, as all teaching elders must be members of the serving presbytery.

title: Liberty granted by exceptions versus right to teach contrary to standards
summary: Ordination with exceptions grants personal liberty to hold minority views but does not warrant public teaching or preaching of those views in ways that disturb the church's peace and purity.

title: Handling exceptions at ordination and distinctions between BCO and confessional exceptions
summary: Courts must investigate stated exceptions; BCO exceptions under vow 3 are handled differently from doctrinal exceptions under vow 2, with judicial process available if warranted.

title: Ordination of men who believe women may serve as deacons
summary: Believing Scripture permits women deacons, while agreeing to abide by BCO standards in practice, is not by itself sufficient grounds to deny ordination or reception in the PCA.

title: Propriety of abstractly listing disqualifying beliefs for ordination
summary: The GA declined to determine abstractly which beliefs disqualify a man from office, holding that only proper judicial processes may make such binding determinations.

title: Relationship of Assistant Pastor to the Church
summary: An overture detailing how assistant pastors are called was found in conflict with BCO 3-2 and 12-2 through 12-4, as the relationship of an assistant pastor to a congregation is best left to the session.

title: Subscription and Stating Exceptions to the Standards

title: Specifying Procedure for Handling Exceptions
disposition: in conflict (majority); minority reported not in conflict

title: Stated Clerk of General Assembly Reporting All Exceptions Taken in All Presbyteries
summary: The overture was mostly not in conflict with the Constitution, but a final sentence risked eroding presbyteries' authority to determine confessional subscription.

title: Subscription and Exceptions of Substance

title: Re-ordination of Former PCA Ministers
summary: The CCB found no technical constitutional conflict but raised concerns about the nature of ordination and inconsistency between restoration after deposition versus divestiture.

synopsis: On complaint from TE David Kniseley and others, the SJC reviewed Rocky Mountain Presbytery's refusal to forbid a mission church from giving an unordained female staff member the title 'Minister of Church Life.' The SJC denied the complaint. synopsis: A church member challenged Heritage Presbytery's ruling that the BCO neither expressly nor implicitly requires a congregation to approve changes in a pastor's call, and that it does not require the session to publicize budget details. The SJC held the BCO silent on both points: once the original call and terms are approved, later changes are budgetary and belong to the session under BCO 12-5b; publicizing the budget is prudent but not mandated. The complaint was not sustained; seven commissioners dissented, arguing congregational approval follows by good and necessary consequence.

synopsis: A complaint challenged Philadelphia Presbytery’s approval of proceedings that cleared teaching and ruling elders without properly trying serious public accusations arising from Christ Church’s division. All three specifications were sustained because plea bargaining, dropped charges, and failure to hear necessary witnesses left the accusations unresolved. Presbytery’s action was annulled and de novo trials produced mixed convictions and acquittals. Harold Burkhart received six months’ suspension, Douglas McCready an admonition, and six former ruling elders three-month suspensions. The decision stressed taking such conflicts to Presbytery or judicial process rather than the congregation.

synopsis: North Florida Presbytery restored a minister deposed for adultery by a 19–17 vote. The SJC sustained the complaint, holding that Presbytery had not proceeded with the required caution and that a bare majority could not demonstrate BCO 34-8’s required strongly favorable general sentiment. It declined to require reordination, calling that question unsettled and treating BCO 37-5’s restoration pronouncement as sufficient pending clarification. The SJC annulled Presbytery’s actions concerning the minister and remanded for a proper probationary and review process.

title: Sherfey v. James River Presbytery
synopsis: Sherfey challenged James River Presbytery’s denial of his complaint and alleged errors in its commission’s proceedings. The SJC ruled the complaint judicially out of order with incurable defects: several grounds had not first been adjudicated by Presbytery as BCO 43-2 required, and the General Assembly filing missed BCO 43-3’s thirty-day deadline. Incorrect advice from Presbytery’s clerk did not excuse compliance. The adopted decision neither reached the merits nor ordered a remand; only a concurrence proposed returning the matter to Presbytery.

synopsis: On complaint from TE David Kniseley and others, the SJC reviewed Rocky Mountain Presbytery's refusal to forbid a mission church from giving an unordained female staff member the title 'Minister of Church Life.' The SJC denied the complaint. It held the BCO uses 'minister' synonymously with pastor and teaching elder, but is silent on general use for non-ordained staff; a lower court may exercise discretion subject to BCO 40-2(3)'s WESP review. The decision addressed only the constitutional issue, not the title's wisdom or propriety; four commissioners dissented.

title: Rev. Thomas Barnes et al. v. Evangel Presbytery

synopsis: The Fifth General Assembly approved its Judicial Commission’s refusal to sustain a complaint challenging Presbytery’s approval of Mercer for ordination as an evangelist without a call and for parachurch work outside its bounds. No reason for rejecting the complaint was stated. The ruling nevertheless required Presbytery to have—and itself issue—a written call before implementing the ordination decision, and requested referral of the broader question defining a valid ministerial call to the Permanent Committee on Judicial Business.

synopsis: TE Kevin Bigelow complained against multiple actions of North Florida Presbytery related to the dissolution of his call as Assistant Pastor of Christ Church East (where he was also serving as planting pastor at Christ Church Beaches). The SJC sustained the complaint in part (22-0-0), finding that Presbytery erred in ruling four of Bigelow's five complaints out of order; however, after reviewing the substance of all five complaints, the SJC denied each on the merits, concluding Presbytery committed no clear error in dissolving the call, that no congregational vote of CCB was constitutionally required, and that no formal discipline without process had occurred.

title: Moehn v. Westminster Presbytery
synopsis: TE Andy Moehn complained that Westminster Presbytery erred in its BCO 31-2 investigation of his wife Kacey Moehn regarding alleged desertion and in declaring the question of biblical divorce grounds moot. The SJC sustained the complaint 21-1-0, finding that Presbytery used an extra-confessional interpretation of WCF 24.6 requiring excommunication before desertion grounds could apply, dismissed relevant evidence, and improperly adjudicated TE Moehn's role in the marriage breakdown without due process; the SJC annulled Presbytery's Recommendations 1 and 3 and found a new investigation was not in order since Mrs. Moehn had left PCA jurisdiction.

synopsis: Teaching Elders challenged Calvary Presbytery’s use of the extraordinary clause to examine and ordain a candidate who had completed only one quarter of Hebrew. The Assembly sustained the complaint’s single specification because Presbytery had not demonstrated either extraordinary circumstances or the man’s proven extraordinary gifts. It found the ordination contrary to the Book of Church Order and remanded for correction. Rather than answer the broader question about proper use of the clause, it ordered a report to the Ninth General Assembly.

disposition: Case returned to lower court with instructions for new hearing; inadequate record
synopsis: Trinity Church complained that Grace Presbytery's July 9, 1976 substitute motion, delaying Adrian Pater's ordination until he was called to PCA work, was an out-of-order reconsideration. The Judicial Commission did not reach the merits: because the BCO 43-5 record was not complied with and minutes were inadequate, it returned the whole matter to the lower court for a new hearing. disposition: Licensure challenge not sustained; complaint sustained as to the unlicensed stated-supply service
synopsis: Antioch Session challenged Peterson’s licensure based on his prior divorce, creation and local-flood views, reversal of a committee recommendation, and close vote; it also challenged his regular preaching before licensure. The SJC rejected the licensure specifications because Presbytery had thoroughly examined repentance and doctrinal adherence, and no definitive PCA standard required exclusion on these facts. It sustained the pre-licensure supply issue under BCO 19-1, 22-5, and 22-6 and enjoined greater future circumspection. The licensure remained undisturbed; the ruling was expressly case-specific.

synopsis: Complainants challenged a Session plan under which most elders voluntarily resigned, the Session granted severance and benefits to its former pastor, proposed about a year with an interim pastor before a permanent call, and contemplated revising local bylaws. The SJC denied all four items. It held that the BCO permitted jointly considered voluntary resignations, that severance concerned resignation and the budget rather than a pastoral call, and that the plan and bylaw proposal were not themselves unconstitutional. Any later call still had to follow the BCO without undue delay, and local bylaws had to remain consistent with it.

synopsis: After Korean Eastern Presbytery tried, convicted, deposed, and excommunicated TE Eliot Lee, the SJC sustained his appeal and reversed the disposition and excommunication. synopsis: Lee challenged Korean Eastern Presbytery’s ratification and filing of a New Jersey lawsuit through a commission acting for the local church, seeking civil adjudication of who was the rightful pastor and who could act as the church’s session. The SJC sustained the complaint and annulled Presbytery’s decision in whole. PCA courts have moral and spiritual, not civil coercive, authority and cannot sue to enforce ecclesiastical decisions. The ruling does not prohibit litigation over purely civil matters and did not condemn the commission’s original appointment.

synopsis: Two ministers appealed Presbytery’s decision to divest them of office without censure after their congregations left the PCA. The SJC sustained the BCO-violation specification and reversed the divestitures: their calls had never been formally dissolved, and BCO 34-10 did not apply because they continued performing ministerial functions and remained accepted by their churches. It declined as unable to judge claims that Presbytery disregarded their emails or used the procedure as discriminatory pretext. The ministers returned to good standing; Presbytery must dissolve their existing PCA calls and then pursue a BCO-consistent option.

synopsis: Mr. Gleason filed a BCO 43 complaint alleging the Session sinned by approving a Personnel Committee Statement read to the congregation regarding an associate pastor's call dissolution. The SJC ruled the complaint judicially out of order and unable to be put in order because BCO 43 complaints are not a constitutionally permissible avenue for processing accusations of individual sin or requiring repentance from a church court, as complaints address errors of courts rather than sins of individuals.

title: Moehn v. Westminster Presbytery
synopsis: TE Andy Moehn complained that Westminster Presbytery erred in its BCO 31-2 investigation of his wife Kacey Moehn regarding alleged desertion and in declaring the question of biblical divorce grounds moot. The SJC sustained the complaint 21-1-0, finding that Presbytery used an extra-confessional interpretation of WCF 24.6 requiring excommunication before desertion grounds could apply, dismissed relevant evidence, and improperly adjudicated TE Moehn's role in the marriage breakdown without due process; the SJC annulled Presbytery's Recommendations 1 and 3 and found a new investigation was not in order since Mrs. Moehn had left PCA jurisdiction.

synopsis: Arizona Presbytery divested a minister without censure for prolonged lack of call after he had joined an EPCEW congregation and notified Presbytery of his withdrawal. The SJC sustained his appeal and reversed the divestiture because BCO 38-3(a) had already ended Presbytery's jurisdiction while he was in good standing and under no investigation or charges. It directed Presbytery to record the irregular withdrawal, acknowledge his new membership, and remove him from its roll.

synopsis: The SJC sustained Psiaki’s complaint and held that the CPC Session erred by ordaining and installing officers elected at a February 5, 2023 congregational meeting where the congregation’s bylaw excluded communing members under 18 from voting. Reading BCO 6-4, 25-1, and 25-7 together, the SJC ruled that all communing members are entitled to vote and that local bylaws cannot impose an age restriction; the “good and regular standing” language addresses censure, not age. The decision did not annul the completed ordination/installation, but required future elections and installations to comply with the Constitution.

synopsis: Members challenged a voting restriction imposed at a congregational meeting. The SJC dismissed the complaint as judicially out of order because BCO 43-1 permits complaints against acts or decisions of church courts, and a congregation is not such a court. It identified other possible routes through a report to Presbytery or review of church records. The adopted decision did not decide whether the voting restriction was constitutionally valid.

title: Dailey v. Heritage Presbytery
synopsis: Heritage Presbytery treated a member's September 2016 filing against her session as a BCO 43-3 complaint and began adjudicating it. The SJC sustained RE Scott Dailey's complaint against that action. BCO 43-3 allows higher-court review only if the lower court denies a complaint or fails to consider it by its next stated meeting. The session timely ruled the filing did not meet BCO 43-1 and did consider it, so neither condition applied. Presbytery's post-November 12, 2016 adjudicative actions were annulled; possible underlying disciplinary matters were left to BCO 31-2 and 40-5.

synopsis: Ruling elders challenged James River Presbytery’s delay in honoring West End’s valid congregational vote to dissolve its pastoral relationship and a three-month salary gift to the pastor. The SJC held that Presbytery lacked a constitutional basis to delay the dissolution, but rejected the challenge to its benevolent use of its own civil funds. Complaints 16-01, 18-01, and 19-01 were judicially out of order; the others were in order. No remand or repayment was ordered. A concurrence cautioned that prompt dissolution is not automatic when objective, justifiable findings support refusal.

synopsis: A church member challenged Heritage Presbytery's ruling that the BCO neither expressly nor implicitly requires a congregation to approve changes in a pastor's call, and that it does not require the session to publicize budget details. The SJC held the BCO silent on both points: once the original call and terms are approved, later changes are budgetary and belong to the session under BCO 12-5b; publicizing the budget is prudent but not mandated. The complaint was not sustained; seven commissioners dissented, arguing congregational approval follows by good and necessary consequence.

synopsis: Complainants challenged a Session plan under which most elders voluntarily resigned, the Session granted severance and benefits to its former pastor, proposed about a year with an interim pastor before a permanent call, and contemplated revising local bylaws. The SJC denied all four items. It held that the BCO permitted jointly considered voluntary resignations, that severance concerned resignation and the budget rather than a pastoral call, and that the plan and bylaw proposal were not themselves unconstitutional. Any later call still had to follow the BCO without undue delay, and local bylaws had to remain consistent with it.

The SJC sustained the complaint. Under BCO 23-1, once the congregation concurred and no sufficient reasons to retain the pastor appeared, the resignation 'shall be accepted' and the relation dissolved; the Presbytery's general BCO 13-9 power did not override that specific provision. The Presbytery had already dissolved the relation on December 7, 1991; the adopted judgment ordered no remand. Three commissioners dissented.

synopsis: After a congregation voted to ask that all ruling elders' official relationships be dissolved without censure, the Session concurred and requested an interim Session. The SJC denied the elders' complaint, holding that BCO 24-6b extends by good and necessary deduction from one elder to multiple identified elders. Dissolution ended their service on that Session but did not divest them of office. Because both the congregation and Session requested it, BCO 13-9 and 15-2 authorized Presbytery to appoint an interim Session. A separate constitutional inquiry was denied without explanation.

synopsis: Complainants challenged Southwest Presbytery's January 1991 actions: withdrawing charges against two ruling elders, dissolving Pastor Pollock's pastoral relationship, and rescinding its suspension of Covenant PC's session. The SJC did not sustain the complaint and affirmed. It held the BCO gives no presbytery authority to suspend a session or act as a Session pro tem without formal congregational consent; BCO 31-1 left the elder charges with the session, so they were never validly before Presbytery; the dissolution challenge was moot after Pollock left the PCA, though Presbytery acted correctly on the congregation's request.

title: Dissolution of pastoral charge outside presbytery's jurisdiction
summary: BCO 23-1 does not apply to non-PCA churches outside presbytery jurisdiction; a congregational vote cannot substitute for that chapter's dissolution process.

title: Call of assistant pastor from another denomination without presbyterial examination
summary: A session may not call an ordained assistant pastor from another denomination without presbytery approval and examination, as all teaching elders must be members of the serving presbytery.

Bigelow v. North Florida Presbytery
synopsis: TE Kevin Bigelow complained against multiple actions of North Florida Presbytery related to the dissolution of his call as Assistant Pastor of Christ Church East (where he was also serving as planting pastor at Christ Church Beaches). The SJC sustained the complaint in part (22-0-0), finding that Presbytery erred in ruling four of Bigelow's five complaints out of order; however, after reviewing the substance of all five complaints, the SJC denied each on the merits, concluding Presbytery committed no clear error in dissolving the call, that no congregational vote of CCB was constitutionally required, and that no formal discipline without process had occurred.

synopsis: Chastain appealed Heritage Presbytery’s 2006 excommunication and deposition. The SJC held the appeal judicially out of order because Chastain had renounced PCA jurisdiction on May 8, 2006. Consequently, Presbytery’s later proceedings were moot and SJC 2005-1 remained in effect. The SJC did not reach the merits. A concurrence questioned the discipline process after renunciation; a dissent argued the majority lacked constitutional authority to recognize unilateral withdrawal and thereby undercut discipline.

title: Larry Ball v. Westminster Presbytery
synopsis: A complaint challenged Westminster Presbytery's denial of a challenge to its May 15, 2001 plan to withdraw from the PCA. The SJC answered no: the Presbytery did not err, and denied the complaint. BCO 25's local-church withdrawal right and the BCO Preface's grassroots principles extend to presbyteries unless expressly excluded, so a presbytery may determine its own membership and affiliation. The plan did not 'act for' local churches; they retained rights to remain in the PCA or leave, and retained property and internal operations.

title: Parks et al. v. Central Carolina Presbytery
synopsis: Complainants challenged a Session plan under which most elders voluntarily resigned, the Session granted severance and benefits to its former pastor, proposed about a year with an interim pastor before a permanent call, and contemplated revising local bylaws. The SJC denied all four items. It held that the BCO permitted jointly considered voluntary resignations, that severance concerned resignation and the budget rather than a pastoral call, and that the plan and bylaw proposal were not themselves unconstitutional. Any later call still had to follow the BCO without undue delay, and local bylaws had to remain consistent with it.

title: Nickoley and Stephens v. Southwest Presbytery
synopsis: Complainants challenged Southwest Presbytery's January 1991 actions: withdrawing charges against two ruling elders, dissolving Pastor Pollock's pastoral relationship, and rescinding its suspension of Covenant PC's session. The SJC did not sustain the complaint and affirmed. It held the BCO gives no presbytery authority to suspend a session or act as a Session pro tem without formal congregational consent; BCO 31-1 left the elder charges with the session, so they were never validly before Presbytery; the dissolution challenge was moot after Pollock left the PCA, though Presbytery acted correctly on the congregation's request.

synopsis: Bowen challenged Presbytery’s attempt, two years after installation, to rescind its earlier ruling and annul local officers’ elections and ordinations without trial. The SJC sustained the complaint: ordination is perpetual, deposition requires judicial process, and rescission was out of order after implementation; Presbytery likewise could not suspend a local elder without due process. But it affirmed that infant baptism and limited atonement are fundamentals admitting no officer exception. The officers remained in office but doctrinally out of accord; voluntary demission or proper process was advised.

The SJC sustained the complaint, holding that the BCO grants no authority for a presbytery to depose a session and act in its place, that suspension requires due process, and that the congregation has an inalienable right to be governed by officers it has chosen.

synopsis: The SJC sustained Psiaki’s complaint and held that the CPC Session erred by ordaining and installing officers elected at a February 5, 2023 congregational meeting where the congregation’s bylaw excluded communing members under 18 from voting. Reading BCO 6-4, 25-1, and 25-7 together, the SJC ruled that all communing members are entitled to vote and that local bylaws cannot impose an age restriction; the “good and regular standing” language addresses censure, not age. The decision did not annul the completed ordination/installation, but required future elections and installations to comply with the Constitution.

synopsis: Members challenged a voting restriction imposed at a congregational meeting. The SJC dismissed the complaint as judicially out of order because BCO 43-1 permits complaints against acts or decisions of church courts, and a congregation is not such a court. It identified other possible routes through a report to Presbytery or review of church records. The adopted decision did not decide whether the voting restriction was constitutionally valid.

synopsis: Bowen challenged Presbytery’s attempt, two years after installation, to rescind its earlier ruling and annul local officers’ elections and ordinations without trial. The SJC sustained the complaint: ordination is perpetual, deposition requires judicial process, and rescission was out of order after implementation; Presbytery likewise could not suspend a local elder without due process. synopsis: Brown challenged Presbytery’s abstract approval of six views concerning diaconal practice. The SJC sustained the consolidated complaints and annulled Presbytery’s action because a church court cannot issue a binding decree apart from properly exercising jurisdiction over specific persons. Constitutional conformity must instead be determined through authorized examination or judicial processes. The judgment deliberately left unresolved whether any of the six views themselves were faithful to the Constitution; the detailed view-by-view analysis appeared only in a concurring opinion.

title: Phelps v. Pacific Presbytery
synopsis: Phelps complained that Pacific Presbytery erred by finding no constitutional irregularities in the New Life Burbank Session's ordination of Lee Irons as a ruling elder, despite PP's earlier refusal to receive Irons as a teaching-elder candidate. The SJC denied the complaint. Under BCO 39-3.3, the Court owed great deference to the lower court's discretionary fitness judgment; the single office of elder does not require identical eligibility processes, and the NLB Session had jurisdiction after Irons renounced OPC jurisdiction. PP's action stood; the SJC declined to decide the NAPARC issue.

The SJC sustained the complaint. Under BCO 23-1, once the congregation concurred and no sufficient reasons to retain the pastor appeared, the resignation 'shall be accepted' and the relation dissolved; the Presbytery's general BCO 13-9 power did not override that specific provision. The Presbytery had already dissolved the relation on December 7, 1991; the adopted judgment ordered no remand. Three commissioners dissented.

synopsis: After a congregation voted to ask that all ruling elders' official relationships be dissolved without censure, the Session concurred and requested an interim Session. The SJC denied the elders' complaint, holding that BCO 24-6b extends by good and necessary deduction from one elder to multiple identified elders. Dissolution ended their service on that Session but did not divest them of office. Because both the congregation and Session requested it, BCO 13-9 and 15-2 authorized Presbytery to appoint an interim Session. A separate constitutional inquiry was denied without explanation.

title: Nickoley and Stephens v. Southwest Presbytery
synopsis: Complainants challenged Southwest Presbytery's January 1991 actions: withdrawing charges against two ruling elders, dissolving Pastor Pollock's pastoral relationship, and rescinding its suspension of Covenant PC's session. The SJC did not sustain the complaint and affirmed. It held the BCO gives no presbytery authority to suspend a session or act as a Session pro tem without formal congregational consent; BCO 31-1 left the elder charges with the session, so they were never validly before Presbytery; the dissolution challenge was moot after Pollock left the PCA, though Presbytery acted correctly on the congregation's request.

The January 1991 filing supplied no supporting reasons as BCO 43-3 required and challenged specifications of error that were not themselves acts or decisions of Presbytery.

synopsis: Bowen challenged Presbytery’s attempt, two years after installation, to rescind its earlier ruling and annul local officers’ elections and ordinations without trial. But it affirmed that infant baptism and limited atonement are fundamentals admitting no officer exception. The officers remained in office but doctrinally out of accord; voluntary demission or proper process was advised.

Session could not bind conscience without scriptural authority, and no express prohibition or proof of falsity existed. Many other specifications were rejected; a concurrence cautioned that such emails are rarely wise.

It rejected objections to discussion, questioning, and the timely submission charge, which could proceed without any determination of guilt.

title: Sang Bai Kim and RE Chan Soo Kim v. Korean Eastern Presbytery
synopsis: The SJC sustained a complaint by two ruling elders against Korean Eastern Presbytery over a disputed congregational meeting (three commissioners dissented). The session was deadlocked and had not called a requested meeting; KEP's administrative commission called and supervised the February 18, 2001 meeting, and KEP approved that action. The SJC reversed both lower-court actions, holding that BCO 25-2 places responsibility on the session and that the presbytery's proper course was to adjudicate a complaint under BCO 43, not act for the session. It declined to rule on the meeting's legal effect.

title: Marshall v. Pacific
synopsis: The 42nd Assembly (2014) disposed of Mr. G. Rick Marshall's appeal against Pacific Presbytery by withdrawal. No separate merits opinion was published, so the source does not disclose the challenged conduct, adopted reasoning, or relief beyond the withdrawal.

title: Parks et al. v. Central Carolina Presbytery
synopsis: Complainants challenged a Session plan under which most elders voluntarily resigned, the Session granted severance and benefits to its former pastor, proposed about a year with an interim pastor before a permanent call, and contemplated revising local bylaws. The SJC denied all four items. It held that the BCO permitted jointly considered voluntary resignations, that severance concerned resignation and the budget rather than a pastoral call, and that the plan and bylaw proposal were not themselves unconstitutional. Any later call still had to follow the BCO without undue delay, and local bylaws had to remain consistent with it.

title: Roberts v. New River Presbytery
synopsis: A congregation member complained that New River Presbytery erred in November 1991 by declining to accept TE Don Post Jr.'s resignation and dissolve his pastoral relation, instead appointing a commission. The SJC sustained the complaint. Under BCO 23-1, once the congregation concurred and no sufficient reasons to retain the pastor appeared, the resignation 'shall be accepted' and the relation dissolved; the Presbytery's general BCO 13-9 power did not override that specific provision. The Presbytery had already dissolved the relation on December 7, 1991; the adopted judgment ordered no remand. Three commissioners dissented.

title: Nickoley and Stephens v. Southwest Presbytery
synopsis: Complainants challenged Southwest Presbytery's January 1991 actions: withdrawing charges against two ruling elders, dissolving Pastor Pollock's pastoral relationship, and rescinding its suspension of Covenant PC's session. The SJC did not sustain the complaint and affirmed. It held the BCO gives no presbytery authority to suspend a session or act as a Session pro tem without formal congregational consent; BCO 31-1 left the elder charges with the session, so they were never validly before Presbytery; the dissolution challenge was moot after Pollock left the PCA, though Presbytery acted correctly on the congregation's request.

synopsis: Teaching Elder Wallace Marshall complained against the same Eastern Carolina Presbytery actions at Fuller Memorial Presbyterian Church that were the subject of Case 90-4, filed separately as a Teaching Elder complainant. title: Melton et al. v. Tennessee Valley Presbytery
topics: higher court authority over local church
synopsis: Complainants challenged the ruling of the session of Westminster Presbyterian Church (Chattanooga) disallowing proxy votes at a December 10, 1989 congregational meeting that voted not to rescind the earlier dissolution and property transfer to New City Fellowship. The SJC denied all specifications, holding that proxy voting was not required under BCO 24-4 or Robert's Rules, and that the congregation's decision to dissolve was within its rights under BCO Chapter 25.

synopsis: Smith challenged Presbytery’s reversal of a finding that an elder’s race-and-IQ views did not create a strong presumption of guilt and its immediate judgment against those views. The SJC upheld the reversal as a discretionary determination, without addressing its merits, but annulled the declaration against the views because a strong-presumption finding required judicial process. On remand, Presbytery was to commence process against the elder or rescind that finding and drop the matter. The ruling did not restrict Presbytery’s ability to adopt general position statements outside an investigation.

synopsis: Session members challenged Presbytery’s order to hold a congregational meeting on officer rotation and its handling of the complaint hearing. The Judicial Commission held that ten days ran from the notice’s postmark and that Bristow and Pastor Vitullo could not participate as members of the reviewing court. It nevertheless upheld Presbytery’s authority to require the meeting: a sufficient petition left the Session no option to refuse, while the congregation retained authority to decide rotation. synopsis: The SJC sustained Psiaki’s complaint and held that the CPC Session erred by ordaining and installing officers elected at a February 5, 2023 congregational meeting where the congregation’s bylaw excluded communing members under 18 from voting. Reading BCO 6-4, 25-1, and 25-7 together, the SJC ruled that all communing members are entitled to vote and that local bylaws cannot impose an age restriction; the “good and regular standing” language addresses censure, not age. The decision did not annul the completed ordination/installation, but required future elections and installations to comply with the Constitution.

title: Dailey v. Heritage Presbytery
synopsis: Heritage Presbytery treated a member's September 2016 filing against her session as a BCO 43-3 complaint and began adjudicating it. The SJC sustained RE Scott Dailey's complaint against that action. BCO 43-3 allows higher-court review only if the lower court denies a complaint or fails to consider it by its next stated meeting. The session timely ruled the filing did not meet BCO 43-1 and did consider it, so neither condition applied. Presbytery's post-November 12, 2016 adjudicative actions were annulled; possible underlying disciplinary matters were left to BCO 31-2 and 40-5.

synopsis: A church member challenged Heritage Presbytery's ruling that the BCO neither expressly nor implicitly requires a congregation to approve changes in a pastor's call, and that it does not require the session to publicize budget details. The SJC held the BCO silent on both points: once the original call and terms are approved, later changes are budgetary and belong to the session under BCO 12-5b; publicizing the budget is prudent but not mandated. The complaint was not sustained; seven commissioners dissented, arguing congregational approval follows by good and necessary consequence.

title: Charles Kim v. Korean Capital Presbytery
disposition: Presbytery and commission action reversed; original jurisdiction belonged to the local Session
synopsis: The SJC addressed whether a presbytery and its administrative/judicial commission could suspend a local session and assume original jurisdiction over charges against a ruling elder. It answered no: original jurisdiction belonged to the session, and a presbytery cannot "act for" a lower court by replacing congregationally elected elders. Preliminary Principle Six, BCO 16-2, and BCO 31-1/33-1 controlled; the commission's interpretation of BCO 13-9 conflicted with those principles. The Presbytery's and Commission's actions, including the censure approved by Presbytery, were reversed.

synopsis: Complainants challenged a Session plan under which most elders voluntarily resigned, the Session granted severance and benefits to its former pastor, proposed about a year with an interim pastor before a permanent call, and contemplated revising local bylaws. The SJC denied all four items. It held that the BCO permitted jointly considered voluntary resignations, that severance concerned resignation and the budget rather than a pastoral call, and that the plan and bylaw proposal were not themselves unconstitutional. Any later call still had to follow the BCO without undue delay, and local bylaws had to remain consistent with it.

The SJC stayed further proceedings and declared the report concluded.

synopsis: A complaint challenged Westminster Presbytery's denial of a challenge to its May 15, 2001 plan to withdraw from the PCA. The SJC answered no: the Presbytery did not err, and denied the complaint. BCO 25's local-church withdrawal right and the BCO Preface's grassroots principles extend to presbyteries unless expressly excluded, so a presbytery may determine its own membership and affiliation. The plan did not 'act for' local churches; they retained rights to remain in the PCA or leave, and retained property and internal operations.

synopsis: A member challenged Presbytery’s refusal, after investigation, to try four elders on favoritism charges and its ruling that her related complaint was out of order because dissolution of her church ended her PCA membership. title: Nickoley and Stephens v. Southwest Presbytery
synopsis: Complainants challenged Southwest Presbytery's January 1991 actions: withdrawing charges against two ruling elders, dissolving Pastor Pollock's pastoral relationship, and rescinding its suspension of Covenant PC's session. The SJC did not sustain the complaint and affirmed. It held the BCO gives no presbytery authority to suspend a session or act as a Session pro tem without formal congregational consent; BCO 31-1 left the elder charges with the session, so they were never validly before Presbytery; the dissolution challenge was moot after Pollock left the PCA, though Presbytery acted correctly on the congregation's request.

synopsis: Two consolidated complaints challenged Philadelphia Presbytery’s licensing and ordination of a candidate who believed Scripture could permit women to hold the deacon’s office but promised to follow the BCO and not ordain women. The SJC denied both complaints and affirmed Presbytery. synopsis: Two consolidated complaints challenged Philadelphia Presbytery’s licensing and ordination of a candidate who believed Scripture could permit women to hold the deacon’s office but promised to follow the BCO and not ordain women. The SJC denied both complaints and affirmed Presbytery. It distinguished subscription to doctrinal standards from approval of BCO practices, applied a three-part inquiry, and deferred to Presbytery on the candidate’s credible vow. Because complainants identified no violated doctrinal standard, no error was shown. The ruling reaffirmed that the BCO bars ordaining women as deacons.

synopsis: Heritage Presbytery treated a member's September 2016 filing against her session as a BCO 43-3 complaint and began adjudicating it. Presbytery's post-November 12, 2016 adjudicative actions were annulled; possible underlying disciplinary matters were left to BCO 31-2 and 40-5.

synopsis: A ruling elder appealed convictions for distributing an SJC decision contrary to Session's will and for allegedly false, divisive statements in an email opposing a pastoral-election proposal. The SJC sustained the appeal, reversed Session and Presbytery in whole, rendered not guilty, removed the indefinite suspension, and restored him to office. Session could not bind conscience without scriptural authority, and no express prohibition or proof of falsity existed. Many other specifications were rejected; a concurrence cautioned that such emails are rarely wise.

title: Crouse v. Northwest Georgia Presbytery
synopsis: A serving deacon nominated for ruling elder complained that his session removed his nomination before BCO 24-1 instruction or examination. The SJC held the session erred by adding an unwritten pre-examination 'vetting' removal and that Northwest Georgia Presbytery erred in approving it: BCO 24-1's sequence—instruction and examination before the session determines eligibility—is mandatory. The ruling reserved the session's sound discretion and the treatment of frivolous or clearly disqualified nominees. The complaint was sustained and remanded for adjudication consistent with the decision.

title: Gendy v. Central Florida Presbytery
synopsis: A member removed from the rolls under BCO 38-4 challenged Presbytery's ruling that she lacked standing to complain because she was no longer a member. The SJC sustained the complaint: standing under BCO 43-1 cannot be defeated by the very removal challenged. Removal under BCO 38-4 is pastoral discipline, a disciplinary case, not a merely administrative act. The SJC remanded to Presbytery to consider the complaint and take the action it should have taken—remand to the Session. The merits of the removal were not decided.

But because MOP had already tried Meyers on April 13–14, 2012, the SJC held further action moot, ordering no additional relief. Adopted by the SJC as a whole, with one dissent.

The SJC denied the complaint, specifically holding that Woodward lacked standing because he was not under Presbytery’s jurisdiction. It also held that BCO 31-2 prescribes no interview requirement or fixed timeline and found no clear constitutional error warranting departure from ordinary deference to Presbytery.

title: Morton Smith v. Western Carolina
synopsis: Smith challenged Presbytery’s reversal of a finding that an elder’s race-and-IQ views did not create a strong presumption of guilt and its immediate judgment against those views. The SJC upheld the reversal as a discretionary determination, without addressing its merits, but annulled the declaration against the views because a strong-presumption finding required judicial process. On remand, Presbytery was to commence process against the elder or rescind that finding and drop the matter. The ruling did not restrict Presbytery’s ability to adopt general position statements outside an investigation.

Presbytery nevertheless had to impose an appropriate lesser censure or remand for one, and lacked authority to mandate transfer to another church. The unappealed heresy convictions remained, but because the members had joined another church, further proceedings were moot.

synopsis: A church member appealed Presbytery’s affirmance of his conviction and excommunication for failing to heed Session admonition and membership vows, including prolonged absence from that church. The SJC affirmed and denied the appeal, holding that all four specifications—lack of reasonable indulgence, haste, prejudice, and injustice—were nonspecific and unsupported. The ruling reserved the session's sound discretion and the treatment of frivolous or clearly disqualified nominees. The complaint was sustained and remanded for adjudication consistent with the decision.

synopsis: A complainant challenged Nashville Presbytery's handling of allegations against a teaching elder. title: Fordice v. Pacific Northwest Presbytery

It sustained the complaint, annulled the denial, and remanded for Presbytery to amend the documents, institute process, reactivate the investigative committee, or otherwise respond directly and specifically to the unresolved allegations.

title: Dunn v. Philadelphia Metro West Presbytery

Because Presbytery had not acted, the SJC complaint was premature; no merits were reached.

Crouse v. Northwest Georgia Presbytery
synopsis: A complaint challenging a session's refusal to advance an ordained deacon's nomination for re-election to the diaconate was denied by the SJC. Northwest Georgia Presbytery had adopted its judicial commission's judgment that the session did not err; applying BCO 39-3(3)'s deference to discretionary judgments, the SJC found no clear error, held formal charges were unnecessary and re-election was not guaranteed, and refused to attribute one elder's questionable retaliation rationale to the session. The majority encouraged prompt communication of reasons. A dissent would apply BCO 39-3.4 and sustain.

title: Dunn and Pesnell v. Philadelphia Metro West Presbytery
synopsis: The complaint challenged Philadelphia Metro West Presbytery’s November 17, 2012 vote adopting its Complaint Commission’s recommendation to institute process and try TE David Swavely. The SJC did not sustain it. Although the record showed possible procedural irregularities—including unauthorized circulation of an earlier complaint—the SJC found no reversible error: presbyteries receive deference on factual records and broad latitude to judge the sufficiency of investigations. The recommendation to proceed to trial stands, subject to later parliamentary action. The SJC did not decide Swavely’s guilt.

title: Sawyers et al. v. Missouri Presbytery
synopsis: Elders complained that Missouri Presbytery erred in its BCO 31-2 investigation by finding insufficient evidence to raise a strong presumption of guilt that TE Jeffrey Meyers held Federal Vision views contrary to the Westminster Standards. The SJC answered yes: MOP erred under BCO 34-5, and the ordinary remedy was compliance with BCO 31-2. But because MOP had already tried Meyers on April 13–14, 2012, the SJC held further action moot, ordering no additional relief. Adopted by the SJC as a whole, with one dissent.

title: Bordwine v. Pacific Northwest Presbytery
disposition: Complaint sustained; presbytery's declaration reversed and matter remanded for counsel or BCO 31-2 action
synopsis: Pacific Northwest Presbytery adopted a report finding TE Peter Leithart's views not out of accord with the fundamentals of the system of doctrine. The SJC sustained a complaint, holding PNW erred because, without formal judicial process, it lacked authority to declare either that the views were out of accord or that they were not. The record still suggested a strong presumption of guilt. The SJC refused complainants' affirmative declaration and remanded with directions for pastoral counsel under BCO 31-7 and possible BCO 31-2 compliance.

synopsis: A ruling elder appealed convictions for distributing an SJC decision contrary to Session's will and for allegedly false, divisive statements in an email opposing a pastoral-election proposal. The SJC sustained the appeal, reversed Session and Presbytery in whole, rendered not guilty, removed the indefinite suspension, and restored him to office. Session could not bind conscience without scriptural authority, and no express prohibition or proof of falsity existed. Many other specifications were rejected; a concurrence cautioned that such emails are rarely wise.

title: Crouse v. Northwest Georgia Presbytery
synopsis: A serving deacon nominated for ruling elder complained that his session removed his nomination before BCO 24-1 instruction or examination. The SJC held the session erred by adding an unwritten pre-examination 'vetting' removal and that Northwest Georgia Presbytery erred in approving it: BCO 24-1's sequence—instruction and examination before the session determines eligibility—is mandatory. The ruling reserved the session's sound discretion and the treatment of frivolous or clearly disqualified nominees. The complaint was sustained and remanded for adjudication consistent with the decision.

synopsis: TE Kevin Bigelow complained against multiple actions of North Florida Presbytery related to the dissolution of his call as Assistant Pastor of Christ Church East (where he was also serving as planting pastor at Christ Church Beaches). The SJC sustained the complaint in part (22-0-0), finding that Presbytery erred in ruling four of Bigelow's five complaints out of order; however, after reviewing the substance of all five complaints, the SJC denied each on the merits, concluding Presbytery committed no clear error in dissolving the call, that no congregational vote of CCB was constitutionally required, and that no formal discipline without process had occurred.

title: Flatgard v. Metro Atlanta Presbytery
synopsis: TE Flatgard was deposed by Metro Atlanta Presbytery on three charges related to conduct during his marital separation and divorce; the SJC sustained his appeal 14-3, finding the Record insufficient to support a guilty verdict and censure on the charges of failing to maintain elder qualifications, failing to love his wife, and failing to uphold ordination vows. The case generated extensive concurring and dissenting opinions debating appellate deference standards under BCO 39-3.2, 39-3.3, and 39-3.4.

synopsis: Teaching elders challenged Korean Central Presbytery’s summary censure of a minister before an indictment was prepared. No mutually agreed BCO 38-1 confession existed, and declining a confession meeting was not immediately censurable objective contumacy under BCO 32-6; subjective contumacy required confession or trial. The SJC sustained five of nine specifications, holding that the committee could not impose requirements lacking constitutional warrant or control an independent mission board; vague allegations and testimony unavailable for cross-examination also impaired the trial. synopsis: Abshire challenged Presbytery’s commission for its appointment, scope, exhortation, summary disposition of two elders’ complaint, and other actions. The SJC sustained only the challenge to deciding the elders’ complaint without BCO 43 procedures and remanded that complaint. It denied the other issues: the commission could conduct the required investigation, the scope objection was untimely, and its exhortation and report were pastoral rather than formal discipline. A separate sixth issue remained before Presbytery and was not decided.

title: Nickoley and Stephens v. Southwest Presbytery
synopsis: Complainants challenged Southwest Presbytery's January 1991 actions: withdrawing charges against two ruling elders, dissolving Pastor Pollock's pastoral relationship, and rescinding its suspension of Covenant PC's session. The SJC did not sustain the complaint and affirmed. It held the BCO gives no presbytery authority to suspend a session or act as a Session pro tem without formal congregational consent; BCO 31-1 left the elder charges with the session, so they were never validly before Presbytery; the dissolution challenge was moot after Pollock left the PCA, though Presbytery acted correctly on the congregation's request.

title: Bowen v. Eastern Carolina Presbytery
topics: fundamentals of the system of doctrine
suspension from office without due process
synopsis: Bowen challenged Presbytery’s attempt, two years after installation, to rescind its earlier ruling and annul local officers’ elections and ordinations without trial. The SJC sustained the complaint: ordination is perpetual, deposition requires judicial process, and rescission was out of order after implementation; Presbytery likewise could not suspend a local elder without due process. But it affirmed that infant baptism and limited atonement are fundamentals admitting no officer exception. The officers remained in office but doctrinally out of accord; voluntary demission or proper process was advised.

title: Chappell v. Eastern Carolina Presbytery
topics: suspension of session without due process
synopsis: Ruling Elder Chappell complained against Eastern Carolina Presbytery's Commission, which had suspended the session of Fuller Memorial Presbyterian Church and constituted itself as a 'Session Pro Tem' without due process or congregational consent. The SJC sustained the complaint, holding that the BCO grants no authority for a presbytery to depose a session and act in its place, that suspension requires due process, and that the congregation has an inalienable right to be governed by officers it has chosen.

title: Marshall v. Eastern Carolina Presbytery
topics: suspension of session without due process
synopsis: Teaching Elder Wallace Marshall complained against the same Eastern Carolina Presbytery actions at Fuller Memorial Presbyterian Church that were the subject of Case 90-4, filed separately as a Teaching Elder complainant. The SJC sustained this complaint on essentially the same grounds as Case 90-4, finding that the presbytery lacked authority to suspend the session without due process and to constitute itself as a 'Session Pro Tem.'

synopsis: South Florida Presbytery deposed a Teaching Elder, suspended him from the sacraments, and later excommunicated him without first assigning him to a particular church under BCO 46-8. The complainant argued that omission stripped Presbytery of jurisdiction. The SJC denied the complaint: BCO 46-8 requires assignment but fixes no timeframe or mechanism; a deposed minister remains under Presbytery's jurisdiction until transfer, and BCO 37-9(a) preserves censure authority. Deferring under BCO 39-3, the SJC found no clear error in Presbytery's efforts. Two concurrences agreed in result but disputed the majority's broad reasoning and deference.

synopsis: Arizona Presbytery deposed TE John Evans without process after considering investigative-committee observations he had not approved. The SJC sustained the joined complaints, annulled the deposition, and remanded. BCO 38-1 requires the accused and court to approve one full statement of facts; Evans could not approve facts presented after he left. But the provision does not expressly require a meeting or detailed discussion. The underlying matter remained unresolved: Presbytery could proceed with or without process, or dismiss it.

title: Fozard v. North Texas Presbytery
synopsis: At issue was whether North Texas Presbytery wrongly denied a complaint challenging Fort Worth Presbyterian Church’s “Special Case Felons” integration policy as contrary to Scripture. The SJC denied the complaint, holding that the complainant did not show the Session violated Scripture or the Constitution and that BCO 39-3.3 required deference absent clear error, leaving the lower-court actions in effect. The decision, adopted 20-1, expressly did not endorse the Respondents’ Preliminary Principles arguments; a concurrence disclaimed approval of the policy, and one member dissented.

title: Frazier v. Nashville Presbytery
synopsis: The SJC denied a complaint challenging Nashville Presbytery's decision not to indict a teaching elder for allegedly sinful teaching on homosexuality and same-sex attraction. The adopted judgment held that the 147-page record showed Presbytery fulfilled its BCO 31-2 investigatory duty and did not show it erred in judgment when it declined process; the complaint was denied 20-0-1. Concurring opinions raised concerns about committee recusal, record clarity, and exegetical uses of Scripture, but they were separate and did not alter the denial.

title: Bumgarner v. Presbytery of the Mississippi Valley
synopsis: A claimant sought BCO 40-5 review of Presbytery’s handling of his earlier judicial case, alleging grossly unconstitutional proceedings and delinquency in failing to investigate his 2012 deposition. The SJC found the application administratively out of order and incapable of being put in order because BCO 40-3 excludes judicial-case proceedings from review and control when notice of appeal or complaint has been given, and he had withdrawn his 2012 complaint acknowledging it could not be resubmitted. It dismissed under OMSJC 9.2(d). The concurrence added that BCO 40 cannot refile a withdrawn complaint or reverse a censure.

synopsis: TE John Hardie appealed his Metro Atlanta Presbytery conviction on three charges of breaking ordination vows and indefinite suspension, alleging seventeen procedural and evidentiary errors. Applying BCO 39-2/3 clear-error deference, the SJC denied every specification and upheld the judgment and censure. It found no clear error in the BCO 31-2 investigation, indictment/prosecutor process, commission membership, evidence rulings, scheduling, alleged prejudice, or censure. It assessed transcription costs equally while encouraging MAP to absorb them, and cautioned that an absent commissioner's vote might support a future challenge.

title: Thompson v. South Florida Presbytery
synopsis: After a Session excommunicated a member without trial for contumacy, the SJC sustained his complaint and annulled the contumacy judgment, excommunication, and later Session and Presbytery actions. No mutually agreed BCO 38-1 confession existed, and declining a confession meeting was not immediately censurable objective contumacy under BCO 32-6; subjective contumacy required confession or trial. He reverted to membership under pending indictment. The SJC did not find the indictment unconstitutional, decide trial guilt, or consider the unpleaded trespass warning.

The SJC denied the complaint: BCO 46-8 requires assignment but fixes no timeframe or mechanism; a deposed minister remains under Presbytery's jurisdiction until transfer, and BCO 37-9(a) preserves censure authority. Deferring under BCO 39-3, the SJC found no clear error in Presbytery's efforts. Two concurrences agreed in result but disputed the majority's broad reasoning and deference.

title: Evans and Pitts et al. v. Arizona Presbytery
synopsis: Arizona Presbytery deposed TE John Evans without process after considering investigative-committee observations he had not approved. The SJC sustained the joined complaints, annulled the deposition, and remanded. BCO 38-1 requires the accused and court to approve one full statement of facts; Evans could not approve facts presented after he left. But the provision does not expressly require a meeting or detailed discussion. The underlying matter remained unresolved: Presbytery could proceed with or without process, or dismiss it.

title: Ganzel v. Central Florida Presbytery
synopsis: A minister appealed a judgment finding him guilty on most charges and imposing six months’ suspension. The SJC held BCO 32-20 barred Specifications 1, 2, and 4 because Presbytery lacked extraordinary justification for prosecuting old allegations, but did not bar ongoing Specification 3. It separately found the entire process constitutionally flawed and prejudicial. The SJC reversed the whole censure, declined Presbytery’s requested harsher sentence, and concluded the matter. A concurrence disputed the majority’s BCO 32-20 interpretation while agreeing with the result.

It declined to require reordination, calling that question unsettled and treating BCO 37-5’s restoration pronouncement as sufficient pending clarification. The SJC annulled Presbytery’s actions concerning the minister and remanded for a proper probationary and review process.

title: Sherfey v. James River Presbytery
synopsis: Sherfey challenged James River Presbytery’s denial of his complaint and alleged errors in its commission’s proceedings. The SJC ruled the complaint judicially out of order with incurable defects: several grounds had not first been adjudicated by Presbytery as BCO 43-2 required, and the General Assembly filing missed BCO 43-3’s thirty-day deadline. Incorrect advice from Presbytery’s clerk did not excuse compliance. The adopted decision neither reached the merits nor ordered a remand; only a concurrence proposed returning the matter to Presbytery.

Harris v. Wisconsin Presbytery
synopsis: RE Harris, as a Presbytery prosecutor, complained that Wisconsin Presbytery's Judicial Commission erred in dismissing both indictments against a pastor for alleged pastoral care failures. The SJC denied the complaint 18-4-0, finding the JC's dismissal of Indictment 1 under BCO 32-20 (passage of time) was within its discretion despite noting some troubling reasoning by JC members, and that the dismissal of Indictment 2 was authorized because the charge arose from a private offense never brought through proper process; four members dissented as to Indictment 1, arguing the JC clearly erred by conducting a de facto trial with only the accused's unsworn testimony.

title: Session of First Presbyterian Church North Port v. Presbytery of Southwest Florida
synopsis: The SJC sustained the Session's complaint against Presbytery. Presbytery had ruled a member's original complaint administratively out of order as untimely but then remanded the matter to the Session; the SJC held that once out of order, no complaint remained to remand. It also held Presbytery could not direct or instruct the Session to initiate formal process without BCO 40-5's required citation step, so those directions were null and void. The member remained under the Session's jurisdiction; the civil trespass order was not ecclesiastical discipline and did not alter membership.

title: Brown v. Northern California Presbytery
synopsis: Brown challenged Presbytery’s abstract approval of six views concerning diaconal practice. The SJC sustained the consolidated complaints and annulled Presbytery’s action because a church court cannot issue a binding decree apart from properly exercising jurisdiction over specific persons. Constitutional conformity must instead be determined through authorized examination or judicial processes. The judgment deliberately left unresolved whether any of the six views themselves were faithful to the Constitution; the detailed view-by-view analysis appeared only in a concurring opinion.

synopsis: The SJC sustained a session's timely complaint that Louisiana Presbytery barred one of its members from the Lord's Table after assuming original jurisdiction. Under BCO 33-1, a presbytery may assume jurisdiction only when the session 'refuses to act'; because the session had investigated and found no strong presumption of guilt, it acted, so LAP never acquired jurisdiction. The censure was therefore a nullity, and the member remained under his session. The SJC also held the jurisdictional assumption reviewable despite no timely complaint against it. Three commissioners dissented.

synopsis: The SJC addressed whether a presbytery and its administrative/judicial commission could suspend a local session and assume original jurisdiction over charges against a ruling elder. It answered no: original jurisdiction belonged to the session, and a presbytery cannot "act for" a lower court by replacing congregationally elected elders. Preliminary Principle Six, BCO 16-2, and BCO 31-1/33-1 controlled; the commission's interpretation of BCO 13-9 conflicted with those principles. The Presbytery's and Commission's actions, including the censure approved by Presbytery, were reversed.

synopsis: Did a presbytery fail in its duty to condemn erroneous opinions by acquitting a minister on theological-error charges? The SJC denied the complaint, leaving the acquittal undisturbed. The record contained the defendant's testimony, including recantations or clarifications, Defense Exhibit 1, and witness testimony sufficient to refrain from contradicting the trial court. synopsis: Teaching and ruling elders challenged Presbytery’s approval of TE Gregory Lawrence’s acquittal on five doctrinal charges. Ruff challenged Presbytery's failure to investigate a teaching elder, but BCO 43 requires a complaint against an act or decision; lack of action qualifies only when a court meeting has occurred and the court failed to act. Incorrect advice from Presbytery’s clerk did not excuse compliance. The adopted decision neither reached the merits nor ordered a remand; only a concurrence proposed returning the matter to Presbytery.

synopsis: Kirk Lyons filed BCO 32-2 charges against TE Craig Bulkeley with Western Carolina Presbytery. Applying BCO 39-3.2–3.3, the SJC deferred to the lower courts' factual and discretionary findings absent clear error. It found no clear procedural error, upheld the conclusion that the wife did not sin by seeking civil protection, and invoked BCO 31-8's caution about accusations from one under censure.

synopsis: A minister complained that his presbytery wrongly refused to order a BCO 31-2 investigation into another minister’s Covenant of Works/Federal Vision views. The SJC sustained the complaint and remanded for that investigation, holding that BCO 31-2 requires investigation of credible, injurious reports about Christian character. A concurrence agreed in result; the dissent found no clear error in the presbytery’s exercise of discretion.

synopsis: Two consolidated complaints challenged Philadelphia Presbytery’s licensing and ordination of a candidate who believed Scripture could permit women to hold the deacon’s office but promised to follow the BCO and not ordain women. The SJC denied both complaints and affirmed Presbytery. It distinguished subscription to doctrinal standards from approval of BCO practices, applied a three-part inquiry, and deferred to Presbytery on the candidate’s credible vow. Because complainants identified no violated doctrinal standard, no error was shown. The ruling reaffirmed that the BCO bars ordaining women as deacons.

synopsis: Members challenged Presbytery’s denial of their complaint against a Session instruction not to circulate an open letter repeating allegations against their pastor. The SJC denied the complaint, leaving the instruction in force. It held that liberty of conscience does not eliminate members’ obligation to obey lawful church injunctions. Here the members had sought the Session’s advice, Presbytery had found no strong presumption of chargeable offenses, and renewed circulation would disturb the church’s peace; under those circumstances, the Session acted within its authority.

Four commissioners dissented, arguing that the presbytery clerk's admittedly incorrect advice, Robar's reliance, and Presbytery's request to treat the appeal as timely should excuse the filing defect under the Plowman precedent and equity or estoppel principles.

synopsis: The SJC sustained a session's timely complaint that Louisiana Presbytery barred one of its members from the Lord's Table after assuming original jurisdiction. Under BCO 33-1, a presbytery may assume jurisdiction only when the session 'refuses to act'; because the session had investigated and found no strong presumption of guilt, it acted, so LAP never acquired jurisdiction.
