synopsis: The SJC sustained an appeal by seven members of a 38-member mission church who were convicted by their temporary Session of opposing the organizing minister's expected election as pastor. Reversing the Presbytery's affirmance and the guilty verdicts underlying indefinite suspensions, the SJC held the indictments fatally lacked BCO 32-5 specificity; Presbytery used the wrong standard of review; the Session had no authority to control pastoral selection; and no Fifth or Ninth Commandment offense was proved. Challenges to witness-judges, venue, and refusal to refer were rejected.

synopsis: A church member appealed Presbytery’s affirmance of his conviction and excommunication for failing to heed Session admonition and membership vows, including prolonged absence from that church. The SJC affirmed and denied the appeal, holding that all four specifications—lack of reasonable indulgence, haste, prejudice, and injustice—were nonspecific and unsupported. It emphasized his admissions that the charges were true, the adequate timeline, and the bar on considering evidence not offered at trial. A dissent disputed his PCA membership, standing, and the Session’s jurisdiction.

synopsis: At issue was whether North Texas Presbytery wrongly denied a complaint challenging Fort Worth Presbyterian Church’s “Special Case Felons” integration policy as contrary to Scripture. The SJC denied the complaint, holding that the complainant did not show the Session violated Scripture or the Constitution and that BCO 39-3.3 required deference absent clear error, leaving the lower-court actions in effect. The decision, adopted 20-1, expressly did not endorse the Respondents’ Preliminary Principles arguments; a concurrence disclaimed approval of the policy, and one member dissented.

synopsis: A member removed from the rolls under BCO 38-4 challenged Presbytery's ruling that she lacked standing to complain because she was no longer a member. The SJC sustained the complaint: standing under BCO 43-1 cannot be defeated by the very removal challenged. Removal under BCO 38-4 is pastoral discipline, a disciplinary case, not a merely administrative act. The SJC remanded to Presbytery to consider the complaint and take the action it should have taken—remand to the Session. The merits of the removal were not decided.

synopsis: In a BCO 40-5 matter, the SJC held that a presbytery erred in upholding a session's erasure of a member who pled not guilty to failing to submit and pursued divorce. The session wrongly equated declining divorce counsel with refusing submission, failed to assess membership duties in another branch, failed to notify her of erasure, and proceeded without process after dropping charges. The SJC sustained the challenge, directed the session to note the notice failure and remove her under BCO 38-3(a), but ordered no express reversal.

title: Memorial of Central Carolina v. Louisiana
synopsis: In a BCO 40-5 memorial, Central Carolina Presbytery alleged that Louisiana Presbytery had exonerated TE J. Steven Wilkins despite his published views on election, the church, perseverance, assurance, and baptism allegedly contradicting the Westminster Standards. The SJC sustained the memorial’s gravity and found Presbytery failed to show due diligence, ordering a recorded examination, formal responses, and report. Presbytery later met the procedural directives, but the SJC relied on Case 2007-8’s substantive finding, cited Presbytery under BCO 40-5, and appointed a prosecutor for Case 2007-14.

synopsis: Members challenged Presbytery’s denial of their complaint against a Session instruction not to circulate an open letter repeating allegations against their pastor. The SJC denied the complaint, leaving the instruction in force. It held that liberty of conscience does not eliminate members’ obligation to obey lawful church injunctions. Here the members had sought the Session’s advice, Presbytery had found no strong presumption of chargeable offenses, and renewed circulation would disturb the church’s peace; under those circumstances, the Session acted within its authority.

synopsis: Black challenged Presbytery’s handling of his complaint and its ruling that a licentiate’s non-24-hour creation-day view was not an exception to the Westminster Standards. The SJC denied remand because Presbytery had effectively adjudicated the complaint; the separate objection to proceeding without Black was not first filed below and was administratively out of order. It upheld Presbytery’s ruling that not every non-Calendar-Day view constitutes an exception. Because the record did not identify the licentiate’s precise view, the decision did not determine its acceptability or whether it could be taught.

synopsis: A church member appealed convictions and excommunication arising from vulgar statements to two patients, challenging the lack of pretrial reconciliation, recusals, the prosecutor’s participation in deliberations, and Presbytery procedure. The SJC left guilt intact and denied a new trial, though it held that a prosecutor may not deliberate as a judge. It reversed excommunication because the record did not show impenitence or contumacy, which could not be inferred from exercising the right to remain silent. It remanded only to impose indefinite suspension from the Sacraments and conditions pending satisfactory evidence of repentance.

The SJC did not sustain either issue. Case 97-9 had reversed only the original censure, leaving guilt intact. Because the offender bore the burden of showing repentance, and Session’s contrary factual determination received great deference absent clear error, the later excommunication remained in effect.

synopsis: The SJC sustained Psiaki’s complaint and held that the CPC Session erred by ordaining and installing officers elected at a February 5, 2023 congregational meeting where the congregation’s bylaw excluded communing members under 18 from voting. Reading BCO 6-4, 25-1, and 25-7 together, the SJC ruled that all communing members are entitled to vote and that local bylaws cannot impose an age restriction; the “good and regular standing” language addresses censure, not age. The decision did not annul the completed ordination/installation, but required future elections and installations to comply with the Constitution.

synopsis: The General Assembly sustained a complaint against Ascension Presbytery for sustaining a candidate's ordination trials despite exceptions to PCA constitutional standards. The Commission upheld specifications that his Lord's Supper and baptism views denied required visible-church membership and that his women-deacons view conflicted with the BCO; it rejected specifications on Sabbath recreation and immersion. It directed correction of the trial and pastoral instruction, with possible discipline if his views persisted.

synopsis: Bowen challenged Presbytery’s attempt, two years after installation, to rescind its earlier ruling and annul local officers’ elections and ordinations without trial. The SJC sustained the complaint: ordination is perpetual, deposition requires judicial process, and rescission was out of order after implementation; Presbytery likewise could not suspend a local elder without due process. But it affirmed that infant baptism and limited atonement are fundamentals admitting no officer exception. The officers remained in office but doctrinally out of accord; voluntary demission or proper process was advised.

A “difference” need not expressly contradict the Standards; Presbytery must independently investigate and classify it rather than accept the member’s assurance or shift the burden to objectors. synopsis: Bowen challenged Presbytery’s attempt, two years after installation, to rescind its earlier ruling and annul local officers’ elections and ordinations without trial. The officers remained in office but doctrinally out of accord; voluntary demission or proper process was advised.

synopsis: Did a presbytery fail in its duty to condemn erroneous opinions by acquitting a minister on theological-error charges? The SJC denied the complaint, leaving the acquittal undisturbed. A complaint against a not-guilty verdict cannot provoke a retrial at the superior court; under BCO 43 the superior court may only annul or remand, not reverse, and the complainant bore the burden to show error from the record. The record contained the defendant's testimony, including recantations or clarifications, Defense Exhibit 1, and witness testimony sufficient to refrain from contradicting the trial court. The SJC expressly did not decide the defendant's actual views. A separate concurrence elaborated deference standards but did not change the judgment.

synopsis: Arizona Presbytery deposed TE John Evans without process after considering investigative-committee observations he had not approved. The SJC sustained the joined complaints, annulled the deposition, and remanded. BCO 38-1 requires the accused and court to approve one full statement of facts; Evans could not approve facts presented after he left. But the provision does not expressly require a meeting or detailed discussion. The underlying matter remained unresolved: Presbytery could proceed with or without process, or dismiss it.

synopsis: Members challenged Presbytery’s denial of their complaint against a Session instruction not to circulate an open letter repeating allegations against their pastor. synopsis: Bowen challenged Presbytery’s attempt, two years after installation, to rescind its earlier ruling and annul local officers’ elections and ordinations without trial. The officers remained in office but doctrinally out of accord; voluntary demission or proper process was advised.

synopsis: Did a presbytery fail in its duty to condemn erroneous opinions by acquitting a minister on theological-error charges? The SJC denied the complaint, leaving the acquittal undisturbed. A complaint against a not-guilty verdict cannot provoke a retrial at the superior court; under BCO 43 the superior court may only annul or remand, not reverse, and the complainant bore the burden to show error from the record. The record contained the defendant's testimony, including recantations or clarifications, Defense Exhibit 1, and witness testimony sufficient to refrain from contradicting the trial court. The SJC expressly did not decide the defendant's actual views. A separate concurrence elaborated deference standards but did not change the judgment.

The Commission upheld specifications that his Lord's Supper and baptism views denied required visible-church membership and that his women-deacons view conflicted with the BCO; it rejected specifications on Sabbath recreation and immersion. It directed correction of the trial and pastoral instruction, with possible discipline if his views persisted.

synopsis: Did a presbytery fail in its duty to condemn erroneous opinions by acquitting a minister on theological-error charges? The SJC denied the complaint, leaving the acquittal undisturbed. A complaint against a not-guilty verdict cannot provoke a retrial at the superior court; under BCO 43 the superior court may only annul or remand, not reverse, and the complainant bore the burden to show error from the record. The record contained the defendant's testimony, including recantations or clarifications, Defense Exhibit 1, and witness testimony sufficient to refrain from contradicting the trial court. The SJC expressly did not decide the defendant's actual views. A separate concurrence elaborated deference standards but did not change the judgment.

synopsis: Teaching and ruling elders challenged Presbytery’s approval of TE Gregory Lawrence’s acquittal on five doctrinal charges. The SJC sustained the complaint on procedural grounds: the trial commission relied on his post-indictment exculpatory writings while he declined to testify, depriving the prosecution of cross-examination. The SJC ordered a new trial on the same indictment under specified evidentiary procedures. Because this was a complaint rather than an appeal, it did not reverse the acquittals into findings of guilt or decide the doctrinal merits.

synopsis: Bowen challenged Presbytery’s attempt, two years after installation, to rescind its earlier ruling and annul local officers’ elections and ordinations without trial. The SJC sustained the complaint: ordination is perpetual, deposition requires judicial process, and rescission was out of order after implementation; Presbytery likewise could not suspend a local elder without due process. But it affirmed that infant baptism and limited atonement are fundamentals admitting no officer exception. The officers remained in office but doctrinally out of accord; voluntary demission or proper process was advised.

synopsis: A church member appealed Presbytery’s affirmance of his conviction and excommunication for failing to heed Session admonition and membership vows, including prolonged absence from that church. The SJC affirmed and denied the appeal, holding that all four specifications—lack of reasonable indulgence, haste, prejudice, and injustice—were nonspecific and unsupported. It emphasized his admissions that the charges were true, the adequate timeline, and the bar on considering evidence not offered at trial. A dissent disputed his PCA membership, standing, and the Session’s jurisdiction.

synopsis: Grace PCA’s Session challenged Ohio Presbytery’s reversal of excommunication for two members convicted of heresy. The SJC partially sustained the complaint: prior indefinite suspension was not constitutionally required, but Presbytery properly found excommunication too severe because the trial record contained no evidence of contumacy. Presbytery nevertheless had to impose an appropriate lesser censure or remand for one, and lacked authority to mandate transfer to another church. The unappealed heresy convictions remained, but because the members had joined another church, further proceedings were moot.

synopsis: A complainant challenged Nashville Presbytery's handling of allegations against a teaching elder. The SJC held the matter judicially out of order and dismissed it, finding the original filing with the church session was not a BCO 43-1 complaint because the session lacked jurisdiction over the teaching elder. synopsis: The SJC sustained a session's timely complaint that Louisiana Presbytery barred one of its members from the Lord's Table after assuming original jurisdiction. Under BCO 33-1, a presbytery may assume jurisdiction only when the session 'refuses to act'; because the session had investigated and found no strong presumption of guilt, it acted, so LAP never acquired jurisdiction. The censure was therefore a nullity, and the member remained under his session. The SJC also held the jurisdictional assumption reviewable despite no timely complaint against it. Three commissioners dissented.

synopsis: Did a presbytery fail in its duty to condemn erroneous opinions by acquitting a minister on theological-error charges? The SJC denied the complaint, leaving the acquittal undisturbed. A complaint against a not-guilty verdict cannot provoke a retrial at the superior court; under BCO 43 the superior court may only annul or remand, not reverse, and the complainant bore the burden to show error from the record. The record contained the defendant's testimony, including recantations or clarifications, Defense Exhibit 1, and witness testimony sufficient to refrain from contradicting the trial court. The SJC expressly did not decide the defendant's actual views. A separate concurrence elaborated deference standards but did not change the judgment.

Because this was a complaint rather than an appeal, it did not reverse the acquittals into findings of guilt or decide the doctrinal merits.

Bound to the record and clear-error review, the SJC found no procedural violation and insufficient evidence that Presbytery clearly erred. It left the verdicts undisturbed, declined to endorse Leithart's views generally, and urged continued clarification of his non-standard terminology. A separate dissent would have found error and ordered a new trial or reference.

synopsis: Biese and others complained that Tennessee Valley Presbytery erred by approving Redeemer Church session minutes without exception—minutes noting a youth Super Bowl party—and by denying their complaint seeking a Sabbath exception. The SJC denied the complaint: because Presbytery gave no reasons for its actions, the record was insufficient to find it erred in interpreting the Constitution. A concurrence said the denial did not decide the Sabbath merits; a dissent would have held the complaint judicially out of order for lack of SJC jurisdiction over presbytery record review.

synopsis: A complainant challenged Nashville Presbytery's handling of allegations against a teaching elder. The SJC held the matter judicially out of order and dismissed it, finding the original filing with the church session was not a BCO 43-1 complaint because the session lacked jurisdiction over the teaching elder. Presbytery properly treated the allegations as BCO 31-2/34-1 reports, and the complainant, not a Nashville member, lacked standing to complain about that new action. A nine-member dissent argued the filing of charges conferred standing under prior SJC cases.

synopsis: The SJC sustained an appeal by seven members of a 38-member mission church who were convicted by their temporary Session of opposing the organizing minister's expected election as pastor. Reversing the Presbytery's affirmance and the guilty verdicts underlying indefinite suspensions, the SJC held the indictments fatally lacked BCO 32-5 specificity; Presbytery used the wrong standard of review; the Session had no authority to control pastoral selection; and no Fifth or Ninth Commandment offense was proved. Challenges to witness-judges, venue, and refusal to refer were rejected.

synopsis: The complaint challenged Presbytery’s commissions and its response to a canceled congregational meeting. The SJC upheld the Inman Commission because a Session may reference limited duties without congregational consent. It sustained the challenges to Presbytery’s consideration of the August 7 meeting and appointment of the Sealy Commission because the Session majority had validly canceled the meeting. Linton’s and Pellom’s calls therefore remained undissolved and Neville was uncalled, absent later congregational action. The SJC also upheld Presbytery’s criticism of the cancellation as unwise and its refusal to issue a BCO 40-5 citation.

synopsis: Smith challenged Presbytery’s reversal of a finding that an elder’s race-and-IQ views did not create a strong presumption of guilt and its immediate judgment against those views. The SJC upheld the reversal as a discretionary determination, without addressing its merits, but annulled the declaration against the views because a strong-presumption finding required judicial process. On remand, Presbytery was to commence process against the elder or rescind that finding and drop the matter. The ruling did not restrict Presbytery’s ability to adopt general position statements outside an investigation.

synopsis: Smith challenged Presbytery’s reversal of a finding that an elder’s race-and-IQ views did not create a strong presumption of guilt and its immediate judgment against those views. The SJC upheld the reversal as a discretionary determination, without addressing its merits, but annulled the declaration against the views because a strong-presumption finding required judicial process. The ruling did not restrict Presbytery’s ability to adopt general position statements outside an investigation.

synopsis: A complaint challenged Philadelphia Presbytery’s approval of proceedings that cleared teaching and ruling elders without properly trying serious public accusations arising from Christ Church’s division. All three specifications were sustained because plea bargaining, dropped charges, and failure to hear necessary witnesses left the accusations unresolved. Presbytery’s action was annulled and de novo trials produced mixed convictions and acquittals. Harold Burkhart received six months’ suspension, Douglas McCready an admonition, and six former ruling elders three-month suspensions. The decision stressed taking such conflicts to Presbytery or judicial process rather than the congregation.

synopsis: Did a presbytery fail in its duty to condemn erroneous opinions by acquitting a minister on theological-error charges? The SJC denied the complaint, leaving the acquittal undisturbed. A complaint against a not-guilty verdict cannot provoke a retrial at the superior court; under BCO 43 the superior court may only annul or remand, not reverse, and the complainant bore the burden to show error from the record. The record contained the defendant's testimony, including recantations or clarifications, Defense Exhibit 1, and witness testimony sufficient to refrain from contradicting the trial court. The SJC expressly did not decide the defendant's actual views. A separate concurrence elaborated deference standards but did not change the judgment.

synopsis: Bowen challenged Presbytery’s attempt, two years after installation, to rescind its earlier ruling and annul local officers’ elections and ordinations without trial. The SJC sustained the complaint: ordination is perpetual, deposition requires judicial process, and rescission was out of order after implementation; Presbytery likewise could not suspend a local elder without due process. The officers remained in office but doctrinally out of accord; voluntary demission or proper process was advised.

synopsis: Did a presbytery fail in its duty to condemn erroneous opinions by acquitting a minister on theological-error charges? The SJC denied the complaint, leaving the acquittal undisturbed. A complaint against a not-guilty verdict cannot provoke a retrial at the superior court; under BCO 43 the superior court may only annul or remand, not reverse, and the complainant bore the burden to show error from the record. The record contained the defendant's testimony, including recantations or clarifications, Defense Exhibit 1, and witness testimony sufficient to refrain from contradicting the trial court. The SJC expressly did not decide the defendant's actual views. A separate concurrence elaborated deference standards but did not change the judgment.

synopsis: Teaching and ruling elders challenged Presbytery’s approval of TE Gregory Lawrence’s acquittal on five doctrinal charges. The SJC sustained the complaint on procedural grounds: the trial commission relied on his post-indictment exculpatory writings while he declined to testify, depriving the prosecution of cross-examination. The SJC ordered a new trial on the same indictment under specified evidentiary procedures. Because this was a complaint rather than an appeal, it did not reverse the acquittals into findings of guilt or decide the doctrinal merits.

synopsis: On a BCO 41 reference, the SJC tried a minister on seven charges arising from allegations of sexual misconduct, bullying, dishonesty, a civil defamation suit, contumacy, doctrinal error, and lack of fitness. It found him not guilty on every charge because the prosecution failed to meet its burden, removed all censures and administrative suspensions, and restored him to good standing. For the lawsuit charge, it rejected a categorical ban on civil suits between Christians and required proof that this suit was sinful.

title: David H. Bryson, et al. v. Presbytery of Central Georgia
disposition: Complaint sustained; same as Case 2 - General Assembly sustained complaint against Presbytery
synopsis: Teaching elders challenged Central Georgia Presbytery’s refusal to sustain a complaint against Liberty Presbyterian Church’s Session for closing a disciplinary matter before taking judicial action. The General Assembly sustained the complaint, adopting findings that counseling, Session discussion, and instruction on discipline were underway before the Session closed the matter and refused to reopen it. It requested Presbytery to assist the Session with appropriate corrections or further action and said both courts should heed confessional teaching on marriage and repentance. The complainants’ requested affirmations were not expressly ordered.

synopsis: Did a presbytery fail in its duty to condemn erroneous opinions by acquitting a minister on theological-error charges? The SJC denied the complaint, leaving the acquittal undisturbed. A complaint against a not-guilty verdict cannot provoke a retrial at the superior court; under BCO 43 the superior court may only annul or remand, not reverse, and the complainant bore the burden to show error from the record. The record contained the defendant's testimony, including recantations or clarifications, Defense Exhibit 1, and witness testimony sufficient to refrain from contradicting the trial court. The SJC expressly did not decide the defendant's actual views. A separate concurrence elaborated deference standards but did not change the judgment.

synopsis: Teaching and ruling elders challenged Presbytery’s approval of TE Gregory Lawrence’s acquittal on five doctrinal charges. The SJC sustained the complaint on procedural grounds: the trial commission relied on his post-indictment exculpatory writings while he declined to testify, depriving the prosecution of cross-examination. The SJC ordered a new trial on the same indictment under specified evidentiary procedures. Because this was a complaint rather than an appeal, it did not reverse the acquittals into findings of guilt or decide the doctrinal merits.

topics: fundamentals of the system of doctrine
suspension from office without due process
synopsis: Bowen challenged Presbytery’s attempt, two years after installation, to rescind its earlier ruling and annul local officers’ elections and ordinations without trial. The SJC sustained the complaint: ordination is perpetual, deposition requires judicial process, and rescission was out of order after implementation; Presbytery likewise could not suspend a local elder without due process. But it affirmed that infant baptism and limited atonement are fundamentals admitting no officer exception. The officers remained in office but doctrinally out of accord; voluntary demission or proper process was advised.

summary: CCB found the Administrative Committee's proposed RAO 10-6 amendment establishing a virtual meeting protocol to be in conflict with the Constitution.

title: Grace: Page 152 is missing. (BCO § 13-10; RAO § 10-14)
Amend RAO 11 and 13 to Disallow Memorials
disposition: not in conflict; Adopted by the CCB
summary: An overture from Pacific Northwest Presbytery to amend RAO 11 and 13 to disallow memorials was found not in conflict and adopted by the CCB.

title: Amend RAO 11-2 and 11-10 to Clarify Who May Submit an Overture
disposition: not in conflict; Adopted by the CCB
summary: A proposed amendment to RAO 11-2 and 11-10 clarifying who may submit an overture was found not in conflict with the BCO.

title: Revise RAO 11-2 to Disallow Electronic Communications Regarding Voting at the General Assembly
disposition: not in conflict but not germane to the RAO chapter proposed; Adopted
summary: An overture to revise RAO 11-2 disallowing electronic communications about GA voting was found not in conflict, though not germane to the proposed RAO chapter, and adopted.

title: Susquehanna Valley: Minutes do not list all specific requirements for ordination.
Does the Overtures Committee have exclusive property over overtures requesting amendment to the Constitution?
disposition: Yes (exclusive property); Adopted by the CCB
summary: The CCB advised that the Overtures Committee has exclusive property over overtures requesting amendment to the Constitution under RAO 11-5.

title: Amend RAO 11-5 to Clarify Process for RAO Amendments
summary: Overture to amend RAO 11-5 to clarify how RAO amendments are made was found not in conflict and adopted 6-1-1.

title: Amend RAO 11-5 to Prevent Confusion and Possible Contradictory Actions on Overtures by Multiple Committees of Commissioners
disposition: creates internal conflict; Adopted by the CCB
summary: An overture to amend RAO 11-5 to prevent multiple committees of commissioners from taking contradictory actions on overtures was found to create internal conflict and was adopted by the CCB.

title: Amend RAO 11-5 to Prevent Confusion and Possible Contradictory Actions on Overtures by Multiple Committees of Commissioners
disposition: creates internal conflict; Adopted by the CCB
summary: A Houston Metro Presbytery overture to amend RAO 11-5 to prevent contradictory actions on overtures by multiple committees of commissioners was found to create internal conflict and adopted by the CCB.

title: Referring Overtures Regarding Committees and Agencies and Ad Interim Committees to Overtures Committee
summary: The CCB found Western Carolina Presbytery's overture to also route agency and ad interim committee overtures to the Overtures Committee in conflict with the RAO, creating irresolvable procedural ambiguity at the GA.

title: Referring All BCO Changes to CCB and Bills & Overtures
summary: The CCB found James River Presbytery's overture mandating all BCO changes go to Bills and Overtures in conflict with RAO 13-1, which permits BCO amendments of a particular nature to be referred to other committees.

title: Whether overtures received on or by April 25 should be officially handled for this year's GA
disposition: Overtures received on or by April 25 are timely per RAO 11-6 (60-day deadline); Adopted 8-0-0
summary: The CCB ruled that overtures received on or by April 25 are timely under RAO 11-6's 60-day deadline and must be officially handled at the current General Assembly.

title: Amend RAO 11-2 and 11-10 to Clarify Who May Submit an Overture
disposition: not in conflict; Adopted by the CCB
summary: A proposed amendment to RAO 11-2 and 11-10 clarifying who may submit an overture was found not in conflict with the BCO.

title: Rules of Assembly Operations
summary: RAO 17-3 requires separate adoption of each committee resolution, superseding Robert's Rules' normal practice of a single motion to adopt the full report.

title: Whether additional nominations from the floor (RAO 3-4) would be allowed if the AC did not bring a Stated Clerk nominee
disposition: Yes — floor nominations are allowed; RAO 3-4 second sentence provides GA right to select Stated Clerk regardless of AC nominee; Adopted 8-0-0
summary: The CCB ruled that floor nominations are permitted under RAO 3-4 even if the Administrative Committee does not bring a Stated Clerk nominee.

title: Amend RAO 11 and 13 to Disallow Memorials
disposition: not in conflict; Adopted by the CCB
summary: An overture from Pacific Northwest Presbytery to amend RAO 11 and 13 to disallow memorials was found not in conflict and adopted by the CCB.

title: Referring All BCO Changes to CCB and Bills & Overtures
summary: The CCB found James River Presbytery's overture mandating all BCO changes go to Bills and Overtures in conflict with RAO 13-1, which permits BCO amendments of a particular nature to be referred to other committees.

title: Permanent Committee Members on Committees of Commissioners
summary: The CCB advised Ascension Presbytery that the term 'permanent committee' in the RAO 14-2 ineligibility provision refers only to the four committees enumerated in RAO 4-2 (see BCO 14-1.12).

title: Germane Amendments to Overtures and Resolutions by Overtures Committee
summary: The CCB found that permitting the Bills and Overtures Committee to amend overtures conflicted with the constitution by undermining presbyteries' right to propose measures to the Assembly.

CCB Providing Unsolicited Advice to Committees
summary: The CCB advised New River Presbytery that it lacks authority to give unsolicited advice to other committees, though the CRPR may make any recommendation within its RAO 16 purview to the GA.

title: Vows Taken by SJC Members
summary: The CCB found SJC vows 4 and 5 'flawed' for failing to reference Scripture directly, and advised amending Vow 4 to resolve the ambiguity with BCO 39-3 and the WCF.

3) Regarding the Number of Members of the Overtures Committee Required to File a Minority Report
summary: An overture amending RAO 15-6.s to revise the member threshold for filing Overtures Committee minority reports was found not in conflict and adopted.

title: Amend RAO 15-6.s by Adding New Paragraphs Dealing with the Content of Minority Reports
summary: An overture amending RAO 15-6.s to prescribe the required content of minority reports was found not in conflict and adopted.

title: Germane Amendments to Overtures and Resolutions by Overtures Committee
summary: The CCB found that permitting the Bills and Overtures Committee to amend overtures conflicted with the constitution by undermining presbyteries' right to propose measures to the Assembly.

title: Amend RAO 14-9.h and RAO 15-8.g to Limit General Assembly Debate
summary: CCB unanimously found James River Presbytery's overture to limit GA debate via RAO 14-9.h and 15-8.g not in conflict with the Constitution.

title: CCB Providing Unsolicited Advice to Committees
summary: The CCB advised New River Presbytery that it lacks authority to give unsolicited advice to other committees, though the CRPR may make any recommendation within its RAO 16 purview to the GA.

title: Amend RAO 16 to Require Reporting on Session and Diaconate Membership and Duties
summary: The CCB found an overture amending RAO 16 to mandate statistical reporting on session and diaconate membership and duties to be in conflict with existing BCO provisions.

title: CRPR Recommendation 9: Amend RAO 16 by adding new section RAO 16-11
summary: The CCB found CRPR Recommendation 9, which adds a new section RAO 16-11, not in constitutional conflict with existing rules.

title: CRPR Recommendation 10: Amend RAO 16-3.b by adding two sentences
summary: The CCB found CRPR Recommendation 10, adding two sentences to RAO 16-3.b, not in constitutional conflict with existing rules.

title: CRPR Recommendation 11: Amend RAO 16-3.e by inserting new subsection 6 and renumbering
summary: The CCB found CRPR Recommendation 11, inserting a new subsection 6 into RAO 16-3.e and renumbering, not in constitutional conflict.

title: Rec. V.6)
summary: The CCB found the CRPR's proposed amendment to RAO 16-3.e not in conflict with the Constitution, adopting the finding 8-0-0.

title: Rec. V.7)
summary: The CCB found the CRPR's proposed amendment to RAO 16-6.c.1 not in conflict with the Constitution, adopting the finding 8-0-0.

title: Advice on proposed CRPR amendment to RAO 16-3.e.5 (recording examinees' stated differences in their own words)
summary: The CCB found a proposed CRPR amendment requiring examinees' differences be recorded in their own words to be not in constitutional conflict.

title: Advice on proposed CRPR amendment to RAO 16-3.e.6 (recording ministerial call arrangements)
summary: The CCB found a proposed CRPR amendment on recording ministerial call arrangements in presbytery records to be not in constitutional conflict.

title: Advice on proposed CRPR amendment to RAO 16-3.e.8 (judicial cases and CRPR review)
summary: The CCB found a proposed CRPR amendment addressing judicial cases and CRPR review under RAO 16-3.e.8 to be not in constitutional conflict.

title: Documenting and Reporting a Minister's Stated Differences with the Standards
summary: The CCB found the proposed RAO amendment in conflict with BCO 21-4 because its reporting requirements failed to cover all possible presbytery responses to candidates' stated differences with the Standards.

title: Subscription and Exceptions of Substance
summary: The CCB found that a proposed overture on subscription was in conflict with RAO 16-10.b, which makes clear that exceptions of substance cannot be ignored by a presbytery.

title: Subscription and Exceptions of Substance
summary: The CCB found no conflict, though a minority held that requiring presbyteries to record doctrinal disagreements would erode their exclusive authority to determine subscription under BCO 21-5.

summary: The CCB found SJC vows 4 and 5 'flawed' for failing to reference Scripture directly, and advised amending Vow 4 to resolve the ambiguity with BCO 39-3 and the WCF.

title: Amend RAO 8-4.h; 17-1; and 19-2 to Specify When Minority Reports Are Permitted
summary: The CCB found that amending RAO 8-4.h, 17-1, and 19-2 to specify when minority reports are permitted in Assembly proceedings is not in conflict with the BCO.

title: Change the Composition of the SJC by Amending BCO 15-4 and RAO 17-1; 3 Amend OMSJC 5.1 and 6.1
disposition: not in conflict; Adopted by the CCB
summary: CCB found no constitutional conflict in a Westminster Presbytery overture to change the membership composition of the Standing Judicial Commission.

title: General Assembly Directions Regarding SJC Decisions
summary: The CCB found an overture allowing the Assembly to direct SJC judicial reasoning was in conflict with the Constitution, because a commission concludes business as the court itself under BCO 15.

title: Allowing the CCB to Take Exception to SJC Case Decisions
summary: The CCB found the proposed overture may have been in conflict with the Constitution due to ambiguity in its use of the word 'records' and the phrase 'any judicial cases.'

title: Rules of Assembly Operations
summary: RAO 17-3 requires separate adoption of each committee resolution, superseding Robert's Rules' normal practice of a single motion to adopt the full report.

title: SJC proposed amendment to RAO 17-3
summary: The CCB found the SJC's proposed amendment to RAO 17-3 to be not in conflict with the BCO, and the Assembly adopted it unanimously.

title: Amend RAO 8-4.h; 17-1; and 19-2 to Specify When Minority Reports Are Permitted
summary: The CCB found that amending RAO 8-4.h, 17-1, and 19-2 to specify when minority reports are permitted in Assembly proceedings is not in conflict with the BCO.

title: Whether Committees of Commissioners may nominate a substitute program coordinator
disposition: CoC may only approve or disapprove, not nominate substitute; Adopted by the CCB
summary: CCB ruled that a Committee of Commissioners may only approve or disapprove nominees for program coordinator, and has no authority to nominate substitutes.
